newsitem.title: UK: Ireland urges Britain not to force march through.
newsitem.headline: Ireland urges Britain not to force march through.

text.p: Ireland on Tuesday urged Britain not to allow a contentious Protestant parade through a Catholic nationalist enclave in troubled Northern Ireland on Sunday.

Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern and Foreign Minister Ray Burke intervened in negotiations about the province's traditionally turbulent "marching season" as Britain held out hope that rival groups might work out a compromise to avert violence.
"Clearly nobody wants to see the march forced through as (it was) last year. Nobody want to see people reigned-in as they were last year," Ahern told RTE, the Irish broadcasting network.

Ahern, who praised conciliation attempts by British Secretary of State Mo Mowlam, was referring to the most hotly disputed pro-British march, which the 200-year-old Orange Order plans to hold through the Garvaghy Road zone of Portadown.
Last year, police stopped the annual Orange Order parade in Portadown but relented after four days of Protestant riots and road blockades.
Minority Catholics reacted furiously, accusing Britain of caving in to mob rule and Catholic gangs clashed with riot police for several days.

Catholic nationalists are planning a counter demonstration to this year's march. Security analysts say that if a stalemate continues Mowlam might ban one or the other, with widespread fears of "standoffs" and violence elsewhere in the British province.
The Irish ministers, in Belfast for separate talks, signalled their opposition to any move to push through the march in the teeth of nationalist protests.
Burke hinted at intense Anglo-Irish fears that a repetition of last year's violence would damage an already fraught search for a political settlement and efforts to get a quick end to IRA violence.

"I do think it would be very very serious indeed if the parade was forced down Garvaghy Road...The Irish government does not want to see the parade forced down Garvaghy Road. It would undoubtedly have implications for many things on this island," he told journalists.
Mowlam, striving to broker a Portadown compromise and avert potential province-wide clashes, said the rival groups still had time to hammer out a deal.

"We still have four or five days, we are still meeting and talking with the residents' groups. I don't accept yet that an accommodation is not possible - because then you get people entrenching and you get the situation building up to the kind of problems that we faced last year," she told reporters.

Ahern, in his first meeting with her since coming to power last week, applauded her conciliation efforts and said he would discuss the parades issue during his first official talks with his British counterpart Tony Blair in London on Thursday.

The impasse deepened on Tuesday when Catholics unveiled plans for nightly roadside pickets and a womens "justice camp" in the run-up to Sunday's parade, in addition to a planned "street festival" in the path of the Orange march.
The parades reach a climax on July 12, the anniversary of a 1690 battle triumph by a Protestant army over the Catholic Irish.
Catholics, who are in a minority in the province, regard the annual processions across the province as anti-Irish and say they are meant to make them feel second class.
Protestants says objectors are motivated by anti-Britishness.
